subsection: 2. Balancing redox equations and the electrochemical series

notes.h: The oxidation-number method: the steps (Higher Level only)
notes.b: Complex redox equations are balanced by making the electrons lost equal the electrons gained. That fixes the key ratio of the equation, and the remaining atoms are then balanced by inspection (by counting atoms and adjusting the numbers in front of the formulas).
points: Recap: oxidation is an increase in oxidation number (the charge an atom would have if its bonds were ionic) and reduction is a decrease. There is more on the rules for assigning oxidation numbers in Oxidation and reduction.
Step 1: assign oxidation numbers to every atom on both sides, so that you can see which atoms change.

Step 2: identify the elements whose oxidation numbers change. One increases, so the species containing it is oxidised and is the reducing agent (it gives away electrons). One decreases, so that species is reduced and is the oxidising agent (it takes electrons).
Step 3: work out the change per formula unit, which is the change per atom multiplied by the number of those atoms in the formula. This equals the number of electrons lost or gained.

Step 4: choose coefficients (the numbers written in front of formulas) for the oxidising and reducing agents, and their products, so that the total increase equals the total decrease. Use the lowest common multiple, so that electrons lost equal electrons gained.
Step 5: balance the remaining atoms by inspection, leaving oxygen and hydrogen until last, because the other atoms are fixed by the electron step.
Step 5 in acidic solution: add H₂O to balance O, then add H⁺ to balance H.
Step 6: check that each element balances and that the total charge is the same on both sides.
notes.tip: You are asked to assign oxidation numbers and, hence or otherwise, balance the equation, and to say where oxidation and reduction take place and which species is the oxidising or reducing agent. Set the working out in this step order.

notes.h: Why use oxidation numbers (Higher Level only)
notes.b: Redox equations often have many atoms and charges, so guessing coefficients rarely works. The method gives a fixed order of working with a built-in check.
points: Complex redox equations can't easily be balanced by inspection alone, because oxygen, hydrogen and charge all have to come out right at once.
Matching electrons lost and gained fixes the key ratio first, and the charge check at the end catches mistakes.
Write every charge correctly, because one wrong charge makes the equation wrong.
notes.tip: Balance the electron change before adding H₂O and H⁺. Adding them first leads to wrong ratios.

notes.h: Example 1: manganate(VII) and iron(II) (Higher Level only)
notes.b: Acidified manganate(VII) (MnO₄⁻, the purple permanganate ion) oxidises iron(II) ions to iron(III). Each step below follows the method in order.
points: Unbalanced: MnO₄⁻ + Fe²⁺ + H⁺ → Mn²⁺ + Fe³⁺ + H₂O.
Mn goes from +7 to +2, a decrease of 5, so Mn is reduced and MnO₄⁻ is the oxidising agent.
Fe goes from +2 to +3, an increase of 1, so Fe²⁺ is oxidised and is the reducing agent.
Equalise: one MnO₄⁻ gains 5 electrons, so 5 Fe²⁺ are needed to lose 5: MnO₄⁻ + 5Fe²⁺ + H⁺ → Mn²⁺ + 5Fe³⁺ + H₂O.
Balance O: there are 4 O on the left, so 4H₂O on the right.
Balance H: 8 H are in 4H₂O, so 8H⁺ go on the left: MnO₄⁻ + 5Fe²⁺ + 8H⁺ → Mn²⁺ + 5Fe³⁺ + 4H₂O.
Check atoms: Mn 1 = 1, Fe 5 = 5, O 4 = 4, H 8 = 8.
notes.tip: Exams use MnO₄⁻ with Fe²⁺ as a balancing question. Show the oxidation numbers first, then the balanced equation, then the charge check.

notes.h: Example 2: copper and dilute nitric acid (Higher Level only)
notes.b: Copper metal is oxidised by the nitrate ion (NO₃⁻) in acid, and the nitrate is reduced to nitrogen monoxide, NO. Here the electron changes, 2 and 3, don't match, so you need the lowest common multiple.
points: Unbalanced: Cu + NO₃⁻ + H⁺ → Cu²⁺ + NO + H₂O.
Cu goes from 0 to +2, an increase of 2, so copper is oxidised and is the reducing agent.
N goes from +5 in NO₃⁻ to +2 in NO, a decrease of 3, so nitrate is reduced and is the oxidising agent.
The lowest common multiple of 2 and 3 is 6: 3Cu (lose 6) and 2NO₃⁻ (gain 6) give 3Cu + 2NO₃⁻ + H⁺ → 3Cu²⁺ + 2NO + H₂O.
Balance O: 6 O are on the left and 2 are in 2NO, so 4H₂O go on the right.
Balance H: 8 H are in 4H₂O, so 8H⁺ go on the left: 3Cu + 2NO₃⁻ + 8H⁺ → 3Cu²⁺ + 2NO + 4H₂O.
Check charge: left 2(−1) + 8(+1) = +6; right 3(+2) = +6.
notes.tip: Cu with NO₃⁻ is a topic examiners set. Name copper as the reducing agent and nitrate as the oxidising agent, using the oxidation numbers.

notes.h: Example 3: manganate(VII) and ethanedioate (Higher Level only)
notes.b: Here the species being oxidised contains two atoms that change, so the change per atom must be multiplied up. Ethanedioate is C₂O₄²⁻.
points: Unbalanced: MnO₄⁻ + C₂O₄²⁻ + H⁺ → Mn²⁺ + CO₂ + H₂O.
Mn goes from +7 to +2, a decrease of 5, so MnO₄⁻ is reduced and is the oxidising agent.
C is +3 in C₂O₄²⁻ (2C + 4(−2) = −2) and +4 in CO₂: an increase of 1 per C atom, so 2 per C₂O₄²⁻ ion. The ethanedioate ion is oxidised and is the reducing agent.
The ethanedioate ion C₂O₄²⁻ is also called oxalate.
The lowest common multiple of 5 and 2 is 10: 2MnO₄⁻ (gain 10) and 5C₂O₄²⁻ (lose 10) give 2Mn²⁺ and 10CO₂.
Balance O: the left has 8 + 20 = 28 O, and 10CO₂ holds 20 O, so 8H₂O go on the right.
Balance H: 16 H⁺ go on the left, to match the 16 H in 8H₂O: 2MnO₄⁻ + 5C₂O₄²⁻ + 16H⁺ → 2Mn²⁺ + 10CO₂ + 8H₂O.
notes.tip: Multiply the change per atom by the number of atoms in the formula: there are 2 C in C₂O₄²⁻.

notes.h: Example 4: iodine and thiosulfate, a fractional oxidation number (Higher Level only)
notes.b: Thiosulfate (S₂O₃²⁻) reacts with iodine, and the sulfur ends up with a fractional oxidation number. This is allowed, because an oxidation number is an average over the atoms of that element in the ion.
points: Unbalanced: I₂ + S₂O₃²⁻ → I⁻ + S₄O₆²⁻.
I goes from 0 to −1, so each I gains 1 electron and I₂ gains 2: iodine is reduced and is the oxidising agent.
S goes from +2 in S₂O₃²⁻ to +2.5 in S₄O₆²⁻, so each S's oxidation number rises by 0.5 and each S₂O₃²⁻ loses 1 electron: thiosulfate is oxidised and is the reducing agent.
Two S₂O₃²⁻ ions lose 2 electrons, matching one I₂: I₂ + 2S₂O₃²⁻ → 2I⁻ + S₄O₆²⁻.
S₄O₆²⁻ is the tetrathionate ion.
Check atoms: I 2 = 2, S 4 = 4, O 6 = 6.
Check charge: left 2(−2) = −4; right 2(−1) + (−2) = −4.
notes.tip: Count 2 I in I₂ when you work out the electrons gained.

notes.h: Example 5: phosphorus and nitrate (Higher Level only)
notes.b: A P₄ molecule has four atoms that all change, so the electron change per formula is large, and the lowest common multiple is 60. This example also has H₂O and H⁺ on opposite sides.
points: Unbalanced: P₄ + NO₃⁻ + H₂O → PO₄³⁻ + NO + H⁺.
P goes from 0 in P₄ to +5 in PO₄³⁻, an increase of 5 per atom, so 20 per P₄ molecule: P₄ is oxidised and is the reducing agent.
N goes from +5 to +2, a decrease of 3: nitrate is reduced and is the oxidising agent.
The lowest common multiple of 20 and 3 is 60: 3P₄ (lose 60) and 20NO₃⁻ (gain 60) give 3P₄ + 20NO₃⁻ → 12PO₄³⁻ + 20NO.
Balance O: the left has 60 O, and the right has 48 + 20 = 68, so 8H₂O go on the left.
Balance H: the 8H₂O supply 16 H, so 16H⁺ go on the right: 3P₄ + 20NO₃⁻ + 8H₂O → 12PO₄³⁻ + 20NO + 16H⁺.
Check charge: left 20(−1) = −20; right 12(−3) + 16(+1) = −20.
notes.tip: Use 4 P in P₄ when finding the electron change. P₄ with NO₃⁻ is a topic examiners set.

notes.b: These equations use the same method with other common oxidising agents. Some are used in titrations (measured reactions between solutions), and you should know them.
points: Manganate(VII) oxidises chloride to chlorine, which is why hydrochloric acid is not used to acidify permanganate titrations: 2MnO₄⁻ + 10Cl⁻ + 16H⁺ → 2Mn²⁺ + 5Cl₂ + 8H₂O.
In that equation each Mn gains 5 electrons (+7 to +2) and each Cl loses 1 electron (−1 to 0).
Manganate(VII) oxidises iodide to iodine, which is used to make iodine for thiosulfate titrations: 2MnO₄⁻ + 10I⁻ + 16H⁺ → 2Mn²⁺ + 5I₂ + 8H₂O.
Dichromate(VI) oxidises iron(II): Cr₂O₇²⁻ + 6Fe²⁺ + 14H⁺ → 2Cr³⁺ + 6Fe³⁺ + 7H₂O.
Each Cr falls from +6 to +3, so Cr₂O₇²⁻ gains 6 electrons, and each Fe²⁺ loses 1 electron, which is why 6Fe²⁺ are needed.
Only some atoms of an element may change: in Cu + 2H₂SO₄ → CuSO₄ + SO₂ + 2H₂O, one S goes from +6 to +4 (gain 2) and the other stays at +6 in CuSO₄, so only that one is counted.
Copper loses 2 electrons, and the second H₂SO₄ is needed to supply the sulfate for the CuSO₄.
The manganate(VII) and iron(II) equation, and the iodine and thiosulfate equation, are the ones used in Redox titrations.
notes.tip: MnO₄⁻ with Fe²⁺, Cl⁻, C₂O₄²⁻ or I⁻ are the balancing questions examiners set. Where only some atoms of an element change, count only those.

notes.b: A half-equation shows only the oxidation or only the reduction, with electrons written in. Building the full equation from two half-equations is an alternative to the oxidation-number method.
points: The same equation can be built from half-equations: balance the atom that changes, add H₂O to balance O, add H⁺ to balance H, then add electrons to balance charge.
The number of electrons in a half-equation equals the change in oxidation number.
Example: MnO₄⁻ + 8H⁺ + 5e⁻ → Mn²⁺ + 4H₂O, where the 5 electrons match the change from +7 to +2.
The iron half-equation is Fe²⁺ → Fe³⁺ + e⁻.
Multiply the iron half-equation by 5 so that the electrons cancel, then add: MnO₄⁻ + 8H⁺ + 5Fe²⁺ → Mn²⁺ + 5Fe³⁺ + 4H₂O.
Either method earns full marks once oxidation numbers have been assigned, whether or not the question says “hence or otherwise”.
notes.tip: Questions ask you to assign oxidation numbers and, hence or otherwise, balance the equation, so either method is fine once the oxidation numbers are shown.

notes.b: These are the mistakes that most often spoil a balanced equation. Each has a simple rule to prevent it.
points: Multiply the change per atom by the number of atoms of that element in the formula: 2 C in C₂O₄²⁻, 2 Cr in Cr₂O₇²⁻, 4 P in P₄, 2 I in I₂. Otherwise the electron count, and so the ratio, is wrong.
Balance the electron change before adding H₂O and H⁺; adding them first gives wrong ratios.
Always check charge as well as atoms; an equation can balance in atoms and still be wrong.
Spectator ions (ions that are present but do not change, such as K⁺, SO₄²⁻, Na⁺) are left out of ionic equations.
Bismuth is element 83, so bismuthate (BiO₃⁻) is outside the first 36 elements and outside the specification.
notes.tip: Keep to compounds of the first 36 elements. A past paper balanced an equation with bismuthate, which is outside the specification.

notes.b: Metals differ in how easily they give up electrons. The electrochemical series ranks them so that you can predict which will react with which.
points: The electrochemical series is a list of metals (and hydrogen) in order of their tendency to be oxidised, that is, to lose electrons and form positive ions in solution.
Order, most easily oxidised first: potassium, calcium, sodium, magnesium, aluminium, zinc, iron, lead, hydrogen, copper, silver, gold (K, Ca, Na, Mg, Al, Zn, Fe, Pb, H, Cu, Ag, Au).

A metal high in the series loses electrons easily (M → Mⁿ⁺ + ne⁻), so it is a strong reducing agent (a good electron donor). For example Mg(s) → Mg²⁺(aq) + 2e⁻ happens more readily than Cu(s) → Cu²⁺(aq) + 2e⁻.
The ions of metals low in the series gain electrons most easily, so they are the better oxidising agents: Ag⁺ and Cu²⁺ are reduced more readily than Mg²⁺ or Zn²⁺.
Metals near the top corrode most easily; gold and silver at the bottom are found uncombined in nature and resist corrosion, which is why they are used in jewellery.
Hydrogen is included as a reference point: metals above hydrogen displace it from dilute acids, for example Mg(s) + 2H⁺(aq) → Mg²⁺(aq) + H₂(g).
Copper, silver and gold, below hydrogen, don't react with dilute hydrochloric or sulfuric acid. There is more on this in Acids, bases and their reactions.
notes.tip: The series is about metals losing electrons (oxidation). A metal high in the series is a strong reducing agent, not a strong oxidising agent. Use the series as an ordered list only; standard electrode potentials are not on the specification.

notes.b: In a displacement reaction a more easily oxidised metal pushes a less easily oxidised metal out of solution. You can see it happen, because the new metal appears as a deposit and the colour of the solution changes.
points: A displacement reaction of metals: a metal higher in the series displaces a metal lower in the series from a solution of its ions. The higher metal is oxidised (reducing agent); the lower metal's ions are reduced (oxidising agent).
Zinc in copper(II) sulfate: Zn(s) + Cu²⁺(aq) → Zn²⁺(aq) + Cu(s). The half-equations for this reaction are those given in Oxidation and reduction.
Zinc in copper(II) sulfate: the grey zinc becomes coated with brown copper and the blue colour fades, because blue Cu²⁺ ions are used up.
Magnesium in copper(II) sulfate: Mg(s) + Cu²⁺(aq) → Mg²⁺(aq) + Cu(s); brown copper forms, the blue colour fades and the solution warms, because the reaction is exothermic (it gives out heat).
Iron in copper(II) sulfate: Fe(s) + Cu²⁺(aq) → Fe²⁺(aq) + Cu(s); an iron nail becomes coated with pink-brown copper and the solution turns from blue towards pale green (iron(II) ions).
Copper in silver nitrate: Cu(s) + 2Ag⁺(aq) → Cu²⁺(aq) + 2Ag(s); grey-white crystals of silver grow on the copper and the colourless solution turns blue (copper(II) ions).
notes.tip: Exams ask you to describe what is observed when zinc or magnesium is added to copper(II) sulfate solution and to write the ionic equation. Displacement needs the solid metal to be higher than the metal in the ion.

notes.h: When displacement does not happen, and how vigorous it is
notes.b: The series also tells you when nothing will happen, and how fast a reaction should be.
points: No reaction happens when the metal is lower than the metal ion: copper in zinc sulfate, or copper in sodium chloride solution, where Cu + 2Na⁺ → Cu²⁺ + 2Na does not happen because copper is below sodium and is less easily oxidised.
The anions (negative ions, such as SO₄²⁻, NO₃⁻) don't change; they are spectator ions and are left out of the ionic equation.

The further apart two metals are in the series, the more vigorous the displacement reaction tends to be: magnesium with copper(II) ions reacts faster and releases more heat than iron with copper(II) ions.
notes.tip: Exams ask whether a given displacement will occur, for example copper in sodium chloride solution, and ask you to explain. A metal never displaces a more reactive metal. Exams also ask which metal is more easily oxidised, justified by an observation.

notes.b: This experiment ranks four metals by testing which of them displace the others from solution. The ranking is then compared with the electrochemical series.
points: Aim: to place magnesium, zinc, iron and copper in order of their tendency to be oxidised, using displacement reactions, and to compare the order with the electrochemical series.
Independent variable (the thing you change): the metal, and so the metal-ion solution it is placed in.
Dependent variable (the thing you observe): whether a reaction is seen, shown by a deposit, a colour change or a temperature rise.
Controlled variables (kept the same so that the test is fair): the concentration and volume of each solution, the size and surface area of each metal piece, the temperature and the time allowed.

notes.b: Each metal is added to the solutions of the other metals' ions, and the observations are recorded in a grid.
points: Step 1: clean each strip of metal (magnesium ribbon, zinc foil, iron nail or wire, copper foil) with sandpaper to remove the oxide layer, which would stop or slow the reaction.

Step 2: place the same volume (e.g. about 5 cm³) of each solution, all at the same concentration, in test tubes (or the wells of a spotting tile, a white tile with small hollows): magnesium sulfate, zinc sulfate, iron(II) sulfate and copper(II) sulfate.
Step 3: add a piece of each metal to each solution other than its own; a metal in a solution of its own ions acts as a control, because no reaction is possible.
Step 4: leave for a set time (e.g. 5 minutes), then record any deposit on the metal, change in colour of the solution and temperature change in a results grid.
Step 5: repeat the experiment to check the observations.
notes.tip: A question on this experiment asks you to describe it and to state how the results relate to the electrochemical series. Give the variables, the cleaning step, the control and the ranking.

notes.b: Counting how many displacements each metal causes gives a ranking, which you then compare with the series.
points: Sample data (expected): magnesium reacts with zinc, iron(II) and copper(II) ions (3 reactions); zinc reacts with iron(II) and copper(II) ions (2); iron reacts with copper(II) ions (1); copper reacts with none (0).
Ranking by number of displacements gives Mg > Zn > Fe > Cu, which matches the order in the electrochemical series: magnesium is the most easily oxidised and the strongest reducing agent of the four.
Write an ionic equation for each reaction seen, e.g. Mg(s) + Zn²⁺(aq) → Mg²⁺(aq) + Zn(s), with a grey zinc deposit on the magnesium.
Zn(s) + Fe²⁺(aq) → Zn²⁺(aq) + Fe(s) gives a dark deposit, and the pale green colour fades.
A larger temperature rise, measured with a thermometer using equal amounts of metal powder and solution, is further evidence that the metals are further apart in the series.
Limitation: no visible change shows only that a reaction is too slow to see in the time allowed; it does not prove that no reaction is possible.
notes.tip: You may be asked for the relative reducing abilities of metals from displacement observations, or to justify which metal is more easily oxidised using an observation.

notes.h: Investigation: safety, sources of error and apparatus
notes.b: Some of the chemicals are hazardous, and several things can make the results misleading.
points: Wear goggles. Copper(II) sulfate is harmful if swallowed, an irritant and toxic to aquatic life; silver nitrate stains skin and is corrosive.
Collect metal-ion solutions in a waste container rather than pouring them down the sink, because they are harmful to aquatic life.
Keep magnesium away from flames.
An oxide layer left on a metal can stop a reaction that should happen; aluminium's Al₂O₃ layer makes it appear unreactive.
Deposits are hard to see on dark metals, very slow reactions may be missed, and different surface areas or concentrations make comparisons unfair.
Diagram: a row of test tubes in a rack (or a spotting tile), each containing a metal-ion solution with a strip of metal, labelled with the metal and the solution.
Diagram: a results grid of metals against solutions, with ticks and crosses for reaction and no reaction.
notes.tip: Aluminium's oxide layer can hide its true position, so clean it or note this as a limitation.

notes.b: You can also work out the order of metals from results that someone else collected, and you can use the series to predict reactions without doing them.
points: Secondary data are results collected by others, e.g. a table of displacement observations from another class or a data source; they are analysed in the same way, so a metal that displaces another from solution is higher in the series.
Example: if metal X displaces copper and lead from solutions of their ions but not zinc, X lies between zinc and lead in the series.
The series predicts reactions without doing them: zinc will displace silver from silver nitrate; silver will not displace copper from copper(II) sulfate.
The most reactive metals (potassium, sodium, calcium) are not used in displacement from solution, because they react with the water instead, releasing hydrogen: 2Na + 2H₂O → 2NaOH + H₂.
notes.tip: Don't use K, Na or Ca to displace metals from solution: they react with water.

keyTerms.definition: The charge an atom has, or appears to have, when its bonding electrons are assigned by a set of rules.
Balancing a redox equation by matching the total increase in oxidation number to the total decrease.
An equation showing one oxidation or reduction, with the electrons written in.
The smallest number that both the electrons lost and the electrons gained divide into, used to choose coefficients.
The check that the total charge on each side of a balanced equation is the same.
An ion that does not change during a reaction and is left out of the ionic equation.
The ion C₂O₄²⁻, also called oxalate.
The ion S₄O₆²⁻ formed when thiosulfate is oxidised by iodine.
A list of metals and hydrogen in order of their tendency to be oxidised, with the most easily oxidised first.
A reaction in which a metal higher in the series displaces a lower metal from a solution of its ions.
The factor that the experimenter deliberately changes, here the metal.
The factor that is measured, here whether a reaction is seen.
The factors kept the same in every test so that the comparison is fair.
A test in which a metal is placed in a solution of its own ions, so no reaction is possible and the set-up can be checked.
Results collected by someone else, which are analysed in the same way as results from one's own investigation.

questions.prompt: Using oxidation numbers, show which species is oxidised and which is reduced in MnO₄⁻ + Cl⁻ + H⁺ → Mn²⁺ + Cl₂ + H₂O. Hence balance the equation and identify the oxidising agent.
questions.model: Mn changes from +7 to +2, a decrease of 5 per atom, so MnO₄⁻ is reduced. Cl changes from −1 to 0, an increase of 1 per atom and 2 per Cl₂ molecule, so Cl⁻ is oxidised. The lowest common multiple of 5 and 2 is 10: 2MnO₄⁻ (gain 10) and 10Cl⁻ (lose 10) give 2Mn²⁺ and 5Cl₂. The 8 O from 2MnO₄⁻ form 8H₂O, which needs 16 H, so 16H⁺ go on the left: 2MnO₄⁻ + 10Cl⁻ + 16H⁺ → 2Mn²⁺ + 5Cl₂ + 8H₂O. Check: charge left (−2) + (−10) + (+16) = +4; right (+4) = +4. The oxidising agent is MnO₄⁻.

questions.prompt: Balance, using oxidation numbers, Cr₂O₇²⁻ + Fe²⁺ + H⁺ → Cr³⁺ + Fe³⁺ + H₂O, and identify the reducing agent.
questions.model: Cr changes from +6 to +3, a decrease of 3 per atom and so 6 per Cr₂O₇²⁻ ion (2 Cr atoms): Cr₂O₇²⁻ is reduced. Fe changes from +2 to +3, an increase of 1 per atom, so 6 Fe²⁺ are needed to match the 6 electrons gained. The 7 O in Cr₂O₇²⁻ form 7H₂O, which needs 14 H, so 14H⁺ go on the left: Cr₂O₇²⁻ + 6Fe²⁺ + 14H⁺ → 2Cr³⁺ + 6Fe³⁺ + 7H₂O. Check: charge left (−2) + (+12) + (+14) = +24; right (+6) + (+18) = +24. The reducing agent is Fe²⁺.

questions.prompt: Hydrogen peroxide is oxidised to oxygen by acidified potassium manganate(VII): MnO₄⁻ + H₂O₂ + H⁺ → Mn²⁺ + O₂ + H₂O. Assign oxidation numbers to manganese and to the oxygen in H₂O₂ and O₂, and balance the equation.
questions.model: Mn changes from +7 to +2, a gain of 5 electrons per atom. The oxygen in H₂O₂ is −1 (a peroxide) and the oxygen in O₂ is 0, so each O loses 1 electron and each H₂O₂ loses 2. The lowest common multiple of 5 and 2 is 10: 2MnO₄⁻ (gain 10) and 5H₂O₂ (lose 10) give 2Mn²⁺ and 5O₂. The 8 O from 2MnO₄⁻ form 8H₂O, which needs 16 H; 5H₂O₂ supply 10 H, so 6H⁺ go on the left: 2MnO₄⁻ + 5H₂O₂ + 6H⁺ → 2Mn²⁺ + 5O₂ + 8H₂O. Check: charge left (−2) + (+6) = +4; right (+4) = +4. The reducing agent is H₂O₂.

questions.prompt: Describe an investigation to place magnesium, zinc, iron and copper in order of their tendency to be oxidised, using displacement reactions. State how the results relate to the electrochemical series.
questions.model: Aim: to place magnesium, zinc, iron and copper in order of their tendency to be oxidised. The independent variable is the metal; the dependent variable is whether a reaction is seen (a deposit, a colour change or a temperature rise). The controlled variables are the concentration and volume of each solution, the size and surface area of each metal, the temperature and the time allowed. Clean each metal with sandpaper to remove the oxide layer. Place the same volume (e.g. about 5 cm³) of each solution, all at the same concentration, in test tubes. Add a piece of each metal to each solution other than its own; a metal in a solution of its own ions is a control. Leave for a set time (e.g. 5 minutes), record deposits, colour changes and temperature changes in a results grid, and repeat. Sample data: magnesium reacts with zinc, iron(II) and copper(II) ions (3 reactions); zinc reacts with iron(II) and copper(II) ions (2); iron reacts with copper(II) ions (1); copper reacts with none (0). The ranking Mg > Zn > Fe > Cu matches the electrochemical series, in which magnesium is highest and so the most easily oxidised, and copper is lowest of the four.

questions.prompt: Magnesium ribbon is added to copper(II) sulfate solution. State two observations, write a balanced ionic equation, and identify the reducing agent.
questions.model: Observations: brown copper forms on the magnesium, and the blue colour of the solution fades; the solution also warms, because the reaction is exothermic. Ionic equation: Mg(s) + Cu²⁺(aq) → Mg²⁺(aq) + Cu(s). The reducing agent is magnesium, because it gives up two electrons and is oxidised to Mg²⁺.

questions.prompt: Equal masses of magnesium and zinc powder were added to equal volumes of the same copper(II) sulfate solution. The blue colour disappeared completely with magnesium but only faded with zinc. Suggest two reasons.
questions.model: Reason 1: magnesium is higher in the electrochemical series than zinc, so it is more easily oxidised and displaces copper faster, releasing electrons to the copper(II) ions more quickly. Reason 2: equal masses of magnesium contain more moles of metal than zinc (relative atomic masses Mg 24, Zn 65), and the reaction is Mg : Cu²⁺ = 1 : 1, so magnesium can reduce more copper(II) ions than the same mass of zinc.
